headlines.description: What to Know Nithya Raman delivered a February surprise when she announced a challenge to one-time political ally Karen Bass in the election for Los Angeles mayor. With 76% of the expected vote in Thursday morning, Raman held a vote lead of 429,450 to 394,796 over the incumbent, who was seeking a second term. The mayor finished with 34% of the vote in the June election with Raman finishing second, good enough to join the November runoff. During the campaigns that followed, Raman — endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America LA — repeatedly said she is running to fix a “broken city” under Bass. Bass, who had never lost an election for public office, attempted to convince voters that Raman was “ready for prime-time.” Click here for more November election results in California. Challenger Nithya Raman will defeat incumbent Karen Bass in a monumental election for Los Angeles mayor between two former political allies that sent a jolt through the city’s political landscape, NBC News projects. Councilmember Raman, 45, held a 52% to 48% lead in a round of election results released Wednesday and widened that gap in a results drop Thursday morning, two days after Election Day. Raman’s advantage of 405,193 to 379,069 votes Wednesday night expanded Thursday morning to 429,450 to 394,796 votes, according to figures from county elections officials. Los Angeles Mayor Source: NBC News Decision Desk Projected Winner 52.1% 429,450 47.9% 394,796 The update with 76% of the expected vote in continued a trend of increasing margins in Raman’s favor since early Wednesday morning. The dramatic turn of events marks a political first for Bass, who has never lost an election for public office in Los Angeles, Sacramento and Washington, D.C. The progressive candidate’s projected victory mean Los Angeles will become one of three major U.S. cities that will be led by politicians with support of democratic socialists, including New York with Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Washington, D.C.’s Janeese Lewis George, who won the mayor’s race this week. Raman had the endorsement of the Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America. The November political shakeup comes nine months after Raman, who will be sworn into office in December, joined the field for the June primary and announced a surprise challenge to Bass. The mayor finished with 34% of the vote in the June election with Raman finishing second, good enough to join the November runoff, at 29%. Former reality TV star Spencer Pratt finished third at 25.5%. In the November general election, Bass’ narrow early lead after the first election night returns diminished hours later with Raman pulling ahead overnight as the ballot count continued into Wednesday. Raman consistently polled well with a base of younger voters, who tend to cast ballots closer to Election Day. Those votes typically show up in results later in the vote-counting process. “When bigger tranches of the vote are counted, you’re going to see that lead grow,” said Dr. Fernando Guerra, NBCLA political contributor, said Wednesday. “I would imagine, given the trends we saw in June and previous elections, that Nithya Raman will definitely be the next mayor of Los Angeles.” The two candidates have not delivered public remarks about the results since election night. It was not immediately clear whether they planned to speak Thursday. At her election night party, Bass was defiant. “Four years ago, you gave me the honor of a lifetime to serve as the mayor of the city that raised me, the city my parents chose to build a life in, and the city I have spent my entire life fighting for,” Bass said. “And every single day, I have carried that responsibility with me.” See updates results for top California elections Raman, speaking at her election night party in Griffith Park, said voters demanded change. “They are angry about a broken status quo and the politicians who failed them over and over again. But change feels good, doesn’t it?” Raman said. “We have so much to celebrate tonight here in Los Angeles. This election is about change, too, a city that was engineered over the last few decades to resist change, and the people right here who said enough is enough, because for too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do. “Our City Hall became a place where we became so used to saying ‘no,’ we forgot how to say ‘yes,'” Raman said. Raman thanked her supporters for refusing to give up and supporting her campaign. “You saw hopelessness and you chose hope because you know that Los Angeles is a city with hope in its soil, a city built on dreams and ambition and a refusal to accept the status quo. The city is the most incredible place in the world,” Raman said. Bass was seeking a second term leading the second-largest city in the nation. She defeated real estate developer Rick Caruso in the 2022 election and had the endorsement of all but one of Raman’s colleagues on the Los Angeles City Council. Caruso said he planned to vote for Bass in this year’s election. Her campaign attacked Raman in the weeks before Election Day over public safety, specifically her stated intent to oust LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell. Raman’s campaign team faced criticism in October when it shared, then removed, a social media video that featured the councilwoman and an influencer. In the video, Raman urged people to stop “fascist liars” as images of Bass and McDonnell appeared on-screen — edits the campaign said were later added without Raman’s knowledge. Raman, of Silver Lake, was born in India and moved to the Unite States as a child. She earned a Bachelor’s degree in Social Studies/Political Theory from Harvard University in 2003 and a Master’s degree in Urban Planning from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). She co-founded the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition and also served in the Office of the city administrative Officer. Before running for council, Raman was executive director of Time’s Up Entertainment. The group aims to combat sexual harassment in Hollywood. Raman defeated incumbent David Ryu in the November 2020 election. Raman has repeatedly said she is running to fix a “broken city” under Bass. She has criticized Bass for pursuing large contracts and projects, such as a billion-dollar agreement to raise salaries for police officers and a costly effort to modernize the downtown convention center. Raman has shared plans to improve basic city services, bolster housing production, reduce the cost of living and support the entertainment industry, among other issues. The two also sparred over homelessness, public safety and housing. Born in Los Angeles, Bass is a 1982 graduate of the University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine Physician Assistant Program in 1982. She was a physician’s assistant who later started Community Coalition in response to the crack-cocaine epidemic and other issues before turning to politics. Bass appeared to be gaining momentum a week before the election when a UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll co-sponsored by The Los Angeles Times showed the incumbent and challenger both with support at 40% from likely Los Angeles voters. Nineteen percent remain undecided, according to the poll. The figures represent a dramatic turnaround from the last Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll in the closely watched mayoral race, which showed Councilmember Raman, a former Bass ally, with a double-digit lead. A sizeable 33% of likely voters were undecided in the previous poll published in late September. Raman was favored by 39% of likely Los Angeles voters with Bass at 28% in the September poll. The drop-off in undecided voters since then likely contributed to the comeback for Bass, who has never lost an election for public office, according to the poll’s director. That decline in undecided voters was significant among conservative voters who supported reality TV star Spencer Pratt in the June primary, director Mark DiCamillo told the Times. In the September poll, 22% of Pratt voters indicated they planned to vote for Bass and 16% said they would vote for Raman. That left 63% of Pratt voters undecided. In the latest poll, 41% of Pratt voters said they plan to back Bass over the candidate endorsed by the Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America. Raman’s support among Pratt voters was at 14% in the October poll. Forty-five percent of Pratt voters remained undecided, according to the poll. The poll released Wednesday was conducted online Oct. 19 and Oct. 25 in English and Spanish with a sample of 2,197 likely city of Los Angeles voters. The margin of error is about 3 percentage points, according to the Times. The mayor’s favorable ratings, which took a significant decline after the January 2025 wildfires, remained low with 65% of respondents viewing her unfavorably. That figure was at 64% in the September poll. Thirty-two percent had a positive view of the mayor, according to the latest poll, up from 28% in the earlier poll.

The mayor finished with 34% of the vote in the June election with Raman finishing second, good enough to join the November runoff. During the campaigns that followed, Raman — endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America LA — repeatedly said she is running to fix a “broken city” under Bass. Bass, who had never lost an election for public office, attempted to convince voters that Raman was “ready for prime-time.” Click here for more November election results in California. Challenger Nithya Raman will defeat incumbent Karen Bass in a monumental election for Los Angeles mayor between two former political allies that sent a jolt through the city’s political landscape, NBC News projects. Councilmember Raman, 45, held a 52% to 48% lead in a round of election results released Wednesday and widened that gap in a results drop Thursday morning, two days after Election Day. Raman’s advantage of 405,193 to 379,069 votes Wednesday night expanded Thursday morning to 429,450 to 394,796 votes, according to figures from county elections officials. Los Angeles Mayor Source: NBC News Decision Desk Projected Winner 52.1% 429,450 47.9% 394,796 The update with 76% of the expected vote in continued a trend of increasing margins in Raman’s favor since early Wednesday morning. The dramatic turn of events marks a political first for Bass, who has never lost an election for public office in Los Angeles, Sacramento and Washington, D.C. The progressive candidate’s projected victory mean Los Angeles will become one of three major U.S. cities that will be led by politicians with support of democratic socialists, including New York with Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Washington, D.C.’s Janeese Lewis George, who won the mayor’s race this week. Raman had the endorsement of the Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America. The November political shakeup comes nine months after Raman, who will be sworn into office in December, joined the field for the June primary and announced a surprise challenge to Bass. The mayor finished with 34% of the vote in the June election with Raman finishing second, good enough to join the November runoff, at 29%. Former reality TV star Spencer Pratt finished third at 25.5%. In the November general election, Bass’ narrow early lead after the first election night returns diminished hours later with Raman pulling ahead overnight as the ballot count continued into Wednesday. Raman consistently polled well with a base of younger voters, who tend to cast ballots closer to Election Day. Those votes typically show up in results later in the vote-counting process. “When bigger tranches of the vote are counted, you’re going to see that lead grow,” said Dr. Fernando Guerra, NBCLA political contributor, said Wednesday. “I would imagine, given the trends we saw in June and previous elections, that Nithya Raman will definitely be the next mayor of Los Angeles.” The two candidates have not delivered public remarks about the results since election night. It was not immediately clear whether they planned to speak Thursday. At her election night party, Bass was defiant. “Four years ago, you gave me the honor of a lifetime to serve as the mayor of the city that raised me, the city my parents chose to build a life in, and the city I have spent my entire life fighting for,” Bass said. “And every single day, I have carried that responsibility with me.” See updates results for top California elections Raman, speaking at her election night party in Griffith Park, said voters demanded change. “They are angry about a broken status quo and the politicians who failed them over and over again. But change feels good, doesn’t it?” Raman said. “We have so much to celebrate tonight here in Los Angeles. This election is about change, too, a city that was engineered over the last few decades to resist change, and the people right here who said enough is enough, because for too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do. “Our City Hall became a place where we became so used to saying ‘no,’ we forgot how to say ‘yes,'” Raman said. Raman thanked her supporters for refusing to give up and supporting her campaign. “You saw hopelessness and you chose hope because you know that Los Angeles is a city with hope in its soil, a city built on dreams and ambition and a refusal to accept the status quo. The city is the most incredible place in the world,” Raman said. Bass was seeking a second term leading the second-largest city in the nation. She defeated real estate developer Rick Caruso in the 2022 election and had the endorsement of all but one of Raman’s colleagues on the Los Angeles City Council. Caruso said he planned to vote for Bass in this year’s election. Her campaign attacked Raman in the weeks before Election Day over public safety, specifically her stated intent to oust LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell. Raman’s campaign team faced criticism in October when it shared, then removed, a social media video that featured the councilwoman and an influencer. In the video, Raman urged people to stop “fascist liars” as images of Bass and McDonnell appeared on-screen — edits the campaign said were later added without Raman’s knowledge. Raman, of Silver Lake, was born in India and moved to the Unite States as a child. She earned a Bachelor’s degree in Social Studies/Political Theory from Harvard University in 2003 and a Master’s degree in Urban Planning from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). She co-founded the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition and also served in the Office of the city administrative Officer. Before running for council, Raman was executive director of Time’s Up Entertainment. The group aims to combat sexual harassment in Hollywood. Raman defeated incumbent David Ryu in the November 2020 election. Raman has repeatedly said she is running to fix a “broken city” under Bass. She has criticized Bass for pursuing large contracts and projects, such as a billion-dollar agreement to raise salaries for police officers and a costly effort to modernize the downtown convention center. Raman has shared plans to improve basic city services, bolster housing production, reduce the cost of living and support the entertainment industry, among other issues. The two also sparred over homelessness, public safety and housing. Born in Los Angeles, Bass is a 1982 graduate of the University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine Physician Assistant Program in 1982. She was a physician’s assistant who later started Community Coalition in response to the crack-cocaine epidemic and other issues before turning to politics. Bass appeared to be gaining momentum a week before the election when a UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll co-sponsored by The Los Angeles Times showed the incumbent and challenger both with support at 40% from likely Los Angeles voters. Nineteen percent remain undecided, according to the poll. The figures represent a dramatic turnaround from the last Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll in the closely watched mayoral race, which showed Councilmember Raman, a former Bass ally, with a double-digit lead. A sizeable 33% of likely voters were undecided in the previous poll published in late September. Raman was favored by 39% of likely Los Angeles voters with Bass at 28% in the September poll. The drop-off in undecided voters since then likely contributed to the comeback for Bass, who has never lost an election for public office, according to the poll’s director. That decline in undecided voters was significant among conservative voters who supported reality TV star Spencer Pratt in the June primary, director Mark DiCamillo told the Times. In the September poll, 22% of Pratt voters indicated they planned to vote for Bass and 16% said they would vote for Raman. That left 63% of Pratt voters undecided. In the latest poll, 41% of Pratt voters said they plan to back Bass over the candidate endorsed by the Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America. Raman’s support among Pratt voters was at 14% in the October poll. Forty-five percent of Pratt voters remained undecided, according to the poll. The poll released Wednesday was conducted online Oct. 19 and Oct. 25 in English and Spanish with a sample of 2,197 likely city of Los Angeles voters. The margin of error is about 3 percentage points, according to the Times. The mayor’s favorable ratings, which took a significant decline after the January 2025 wildfires, remained low with 65% of respondents viewing her unfavorably. That figure was at 64% in the September poll. Thirty-two percent had a positive view of the mayor, according to the latest poll, up from 28% in the earlier poll.

The mayor finished with 34% of the vote in the June election with Raman finishing second, good enough to join the November runoff. During the campaigns that followed, Raman — endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America LA — repeatedly said she is running to fix a “broken city” under Bass. Bass, who had never lost an election for public office, attempted to convince voters that Raman was “ready for prime-time.” Click here for more November election results in California. Challenger Nithya Raman will defeat incumbent Karen Bass in a monumental election for Los Angeles mayor between two former political allies that sent a jolt through the city’s political landscape, NBC News projects. Councilmember Raman, 45, held a 52% to 48% lead in a round of election results released Wednesday and widened that gap in a results drop Thursday morning, two days after Election Day. Raman’s advantage of 405,193 to 379,069 votes Wednesday night expanded Thursday morning to 429,450 to 394,796 votes, according to figures from county elections officials. Los Angeles Mayor Source: NBC News Decision Desk Projected Winner 52.1% 429,450 47.9% 394,796 The update with 76% of the expected vote in continued a trend of increasing margins in Raman’s favor since early Wednesday morning. The dramatic turn of events marks a political first for Bass, who has never lost an election for public office in Los Angeles, Sacramento and Washington, D.C. The progressive candidate’s projected victory mean Los Angeles will become one of three major U.S. cities that will be led by politicians with support of democratic socialists, including New York with Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Washington, D.C.’s Janeese Lewis George, who won the mayor’s race this week. Raman had the endorsement of the Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America. The November political shakeup comes nine months after Raman, who will be sworn into office in December, joined the field for the June primary and announced a surprise challenge to Bass. The mayor finished with 34% of the vote in the June election with Raman finishing second, good enough to join the November runoff, at 29%. Former reality TV star Spencer Pratt finished third at 25.5%. In the November general election, Bass’ narrow early lead after the first election night returns diminished hours later with Raman pulling ahead overnight as the ballot count continued into Wednesday. Raman consistently polled well with a base of younger voters, who tend to cast ballots closer to Election Day. Those votes typically show up in results later in the vote-counting process. “When bigger tranches of the vote are counted, you’re going to see that lead grow,” said Dr. Fernando Guerra, NBCLA political contributor, said Wednesday. “I would imagine, given the trends we saw in June and previous elections, that Nithya Raman will definitely be the next mayor of Los Angeles.” The two candidates have not delivered public remarks about the results since election night. It was not immediately clear whether they planned to speak Thursday. At her election night party, Bass was defiant. “Four years ago, you gave me the honor of a lifetime to serve as the mayor of the city that raised me, the city my parents chose to build a life in, and the city I have spent my entire life fighting for,” Bass said. “And every single day, I have carried that responsibility with me.” See updates results for top California elections Raman, speaking at her election night party in Griffith Park, said voters demanded change. “They are angry about a broken status quo and the politicians who failed them over and over again. But change feels good, doesn’t it?” Raman said. “We have so much to celebrate tonight here in Los Angeles. This election is about change, too, a city that was engineered over the last few decades to resist change, and the people right here who said enough is enough, because for too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do. “Our City Hall became a place where we became so used to saying ‘no,’ we forgot how to say ‘yes,'” Raman said. Raman thanked her supporters for refusing to give up and supporting her campaign. “You saw hopelessness and you chose hope because you know that Los Angeles is a city with hope in its soil, a city built on dreams and ambition and a refusal to accept the status quo. The city is the most incredible place in the world,” Raman said. Bass was seeking a second term leading the second-largest city in the nation. She defeated real estate developer Rick Caruso in the 2022 election and had the endorsement of all but one of Raman’s colleagues on the Los Angeles City Council. Caruso said he planned to vote for Bass in this year’s election. Her campaign attacked Raman in the weeks before Election Day over public safety, specifically her stated intent to oust LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell. Raman’s campaign team faced criticism in October when it shared, then removed, a social media video that featured the councilwoman and an influencer. In the video, Raman urged people to stop “fascist liars” as images of Bass and McDonnell appeared on-screen — edits the campaign said were later added without Raman’s knowledge. Raman, of Silver Lake, was born in India and moved to the Unite States as a child. She earned a Bachelor’s degree in Social Studies/Political Theory from Harvard University in 2003 and a Master’s degree in Urban Planning from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). She co-founded the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition and also served in the Office of the city administrative Officer. Before running for council, Raman was executive director of Time’s Up Entertainment. The group aims to combat sexual harassment in Hollywood. Raman defeated incumbent David Ryu in the November 2020 election. Raman has repeatedly said she is running to fix a “broken city” under Bass. She has criticized Bass for pursuing large contracts and projects, such as a billion-dollar agreement to raise salaries for police officers and a costly effort to modernize the downtown convention center. Raman has shared plans to improve basic city services, bolster housing production, reduce the cost of living and support the entertainment industry, among other issues. The two also sparred over homelessness, public safety and housing. Born in Los Angeles, Bass is a 1982 graduate of the University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine Physician Assistant Program in 1982. She was a physician’s assistant who later started Community Coalition in response to the crack-cocaine epidemic and other issues before turning to politics. Bass appeared to be gaining momentum a week before the election when a UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll co-sponsored by The Los Angeles Times showed the incumbent and challenger both with support at 40% from likely Los Angeles voters. Nineteen percent remain undecided, according to the poll. The figures represent a dramatic turnaround from the last Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll in the closely watched mayoral race, which showed Councilmember Raman, a former Bass ally, with a double-digit lead. A sizeable 33% of likely voters were undecided in the previous poll published in late September. Raman was favored by 39% of likely Los Angeles voters with Bass at 28% in the September poll. The drop-off in undecided voters since then likely contributed to the comeback for Bass, who has never lost an election for public office, according to the poll’s director. That decline in undecided voters was significant among conservative voters who supported reality TV star Spencer Pratt in the June primary, director Mark DiCamillo told the Times. In the September poll, 22% of Pratt voters indicated they planned to vote for Bass and 16% said they would vote for Raman. That left 63% of Pratt voters undecided. In the latest poll, 41% of Pratt voters said they plan to back Bass over the candidate endorsed by the Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America. Raman’s support among Pratt voters was at 14% in the October poll. Forty-five percent of Pratt voters remained undecided, according to the poll. The poll released Wednesday was conducted online Oct. 19 and Oct. 25 in English and Spanish with a sample of 2,197 likely city of Los Angeles voters. The margin of error is about 3 percentage points, according to the Times. The mayor’s favorable ratings, which took a significant decline after the January 2025 wildfires, remained low with 65% of respondents viewing her unfavorably. That figure was at 64% in the September poll. Thirty-two percent had a positive view of the mayor, according to the latest poll, up from 28% in the earlier poll.
